turns.response_html:
You don't need to drop $150 on a commercial setup to dry TPU for your Bambu Lab A1. Your instinct to build or rig up something yourself is entirely doable, but a simple wrap with desiccant won't quite cut it for TPU.

Because TPU is highly hygroscopic (it aggressively drinks moisture from the air), the water molecules actually form weak chemical bonds with the polymer chains. A passive fan or just desiccant packets at room temperature can't break those bonds; you need active heat to drive the moisture out.

Here is how you can achieve this effectively without breaking the bank, using a few DIY methods that work perfectly for an A1 setup.

The "Free" Method: The Heated Bed Hack

Since you have an A1, you already own a massive, precisely controlled heating element: your printer's heatbed.

  • How it works: You place the TPU spool directly on the heated bed, cover it to trap the heat, and let the bed cook off the moisture.
  • The Setup: 1. Place the spool flat on the print bed. 2. Cover the spool with a cardboard filament box (the one your filament came in works perfectly). 3. Poke a few small holes in the top of the cardboard box so the rising moisture can actually escape.
  • Settings for TPU: Set your bed temperature to $50^\circ\text{C}$ to $55^\circ\text{C}$ and let it sit for 6 to 12 hours.

⚠️ Warning: Do not exceed $60^\circ\text{C}$, or you risk softening the plastic spool itself or causing the TPU strands to fuse together.

The $30 to $40 Method: The Food Dehydrator DIY

If you don't want to tie up your printer for 12 hours just to dry filament, the absolute best budget DIY route is buying a cheap, round food dehydrator (like a Nesco or a generic brand) from a thrift store or online.

+-----------------------------------+
|        Dehydrator Lid             |
+-----------------------------------+
|      [ Cut-out Trays ]            |  <-- Snip the plastic mesh out
|   +---------------------------+   |      of the middle trays to create
|   |    TPU Filament Spool     |   |      an open vertical chamber
|   +---------------------------+   |
+-----------------------------------+
|        Heating Base / Fan         |
+-----------------------------------+
  • The Build: Buy a model with stackable trays. Take a pair of wire cutters and snip out the plastic mesh grids from the center of the middle trays, leaving just the outer rings. This creates a perfect, heated vertical chamber that fits a standard 1kg spool.
  • Why it's great: They have built-in heating elements and active fans that constantly circulate dry, warm air and exhaust the humid air.
  • Settings: Run it at $50^\circ\text{C}$ to $55^\circ\text{C}$ for about 4 to 6 hours.

The Storage Solution: Dry Box for Printing

Once the TPU is dry, if you leave it sitting out on the A1's stock spool holder, it will start absorbing moisture again within a few hours (especially in humid summer months).

To prevent this, you can build a cheap Passive Dry Box to print out of:

  1. Buy a cheap gasket-sealed plastic storage bin (like a Sterilite gasket box).
  2. Toss a massive amount of rechargeable silica gel beads (or a cheap dry-room dehumidifier tub like DampRid) into the bottom.
  3. Throw your spool on some 3D-printed rollers inside the box, and run a piece of PTFE tubing through a small hole in the box directly to your A1's extruder.

This keeps the filament at <20% humidity while you print, ensuring those long TPU prints don't start stringing halfway through.
